lines.text: Welcome to Money Smart! Today you will find out where money came from, count rupees like a shopkeeper, and give the right change.
Long ago, people swapped things they had for things they needed.
A farmer could swap a sack of rice for a clay pot.
This kind of swapping is called barter.
What if the potter did not want rice?
Then there was no swap at all.
And nobody could agree how many pots one goat was worth.
Money fixed this, because everyone agrees it has value.
More than 2,500 years ago, India made some of the first coins in the world.
Today we use coins of ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10 and ₹20, and notes of ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100, ₹200 and ₹500.
Many families also pay with a phone using UPI, or with a bank card.
The money moves from one bank account to another without any notes changing hands.
It is still real money, so we spend it just as carefully.
Change is the money you get back when you pay more than the price.
To find it, count up from the price to the money you paid.
Always count your change before you leave the counter.
To count money quickly, always start with the biggest note and work down.
Here we have a hundred rupee note, a fifty rupee note, two ten rupee notes and a five rupee coin.
We count one hundred, one hundred and fifty, one hundred and sixty, one hundred and seventy.
Then the coin makes one hundred and seventy five rupees, and we say the total out loud.
Meera buys a pencil box for thirty five rupees and pays with a fifty rupee note.
The shopkeeper starts at the price and counts up to the money Meera paid.
A five rupee coin makes forty, and a ten rupee coin makes fifty.
So the change is fifteen rupees, and Meera counts it again before she leaves.
Kabir buys biscuits for twenty five rupees and pays with a one hundred rupee note.
The shopkeeper is busy and gives him back sixty five rupees.
Counting up from twenty five to one hundred makes seventy five rupees, not sixty five.
Kabir politely says, uncle, I think I should get ten rupees more, and the shopkeeper thanks him.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now build along, then try the challenges. You’ve got this!
